title: South Korean Talent Eases Japan's Labor Shortage
paragraphs: Japan is facing a serious shortage of workers as its population ages. At the same time, many young people in South Korea are struggling to find good jobs. As a result, a growing number of young South Koreans are moving to Japan for work.

According to the Korea Labor Institute, more than 80,000 South Koreans now work in Japan, often in retail, information technology (IT) and game development. Last year, 2,257 young South Koreans found jobs in Japan through government-supported programs, a 47% increase from 2024. Japan is now the most popular overseas destination for these programs.

There are several reasons for the trend. In South Korea, there are not enough good entry-level jobs, because employers often prefer experienced workers and older employees are staying in their jobs longer. South Korea's youth unemployment rate was 7.0% in June, while Japan's overall unemployment rate was just 2.5%.

Japanese companies, meanwhile, are struggling to fill their graduate training programs. Many young South Koreans are attracted by the on-the-job training that Japanese firms offer, which Korean companies rarely provide for new graduates.

Several businesses are helping to connect the two sides. One of them is KOREC, a startup founded in 2019 by Moe Kasugai, a Japanese woman who studied at Yonsei University in Seoul. She said she was surprised that many talented Korean graduates could not find jobs. Japanese companies are also visiting job fairs in Seoul to recruit Korean students.

Employers seem impressed. Tomoya Hattori, the head of a Japanese consulting company, praised Korean candidates for their competitiveness, speed and hard work. Lee Chang-min, a professor at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, said the quality of Korean candidates is very high in terms of language and culture.

However, there are some challenges. South Korean workers often change jobs to get promotions or better pay, while many Japanese companies are used to employees staying for their whole careers. Kasugai believes Japanese companies will adapt, since young Japanese people are also changing jobs more often.
